Right now, more than 90% of AI-driven sales are miscredited as branded search, direct traffic or retail media, according to Similarweb. The IAB has proposed a solution: The AI-Era Attribution Blueprint. It establishes three different types of AI-attributable conversion: human-owned, AI-assisted or AI-executed. A human-owned conversion is when AI didn’t substantively create the purchase intent, influence the product decision or carry out the purchase; however, an AI assistant may still have been involved in the decision-making process. AI-assisted conversions involve the AI narrowing down and suggesting options. The IAB proposes two sub-types: “AI-influenced” conversions in which the AI “shapes intent” but a human makes the final choice, and “AI-recommended” conversions in which the AI “shapes the choice itself.” And AI-executed conversions involve a human giving an agent permission to purchase an item. There are two sub-types of AI-executed conversions, too: one in which the human has told the AI specifically what to buy and one in which the AI makes the selection. If all that sounds a bit ambiguous and not exactly suited to how programmatic measurement works, well, you’re right. But the IAB’s aim at this stage is just to describe how these AI experiences play out in practice, said Caroline Giegerich, IAB’s VP of AI, during a webinar on agentic advertising on Monday. “We define this based on what’s actually happening,” she said, “not what we can measure, per se, today.” Premium Blend Speaking of the IAB, the organization hosted its “I Want My CTV” event in New York City yesterday. But, he added, the “premium” classification is ultimately less important than finding content – or, more accurately, audiences – that fulfill the buyer’s performance goals. But the next mass attention moment for American media – the Super Bowl – won’t be a friendly environment for these platforms, Adweek reports. Although the NFL, like most pro sports leagues, enthusiastically embraced sports betting partnerships and marketing, it’s nevertheless sticking with the prediction market ad ban it put in place for last season’s Super Bowl. The NFL even clarified ahead of this season that its sportsbook marketing partners DraftKings, FanDuel and Fanatics can’t promote their own prediction market offerings during NFL games. Those same sportsbooks launched Kalshi and Polymarket alternatives this year as competition heated up between unabashed gambling apps and “we swear we’re not gambling” prediction markets. These gambling apps now default to prediction market mode in states that prohibit sports betting. It’s a cheeky move. Gambling apps are now using the same argument as prediction markets to sidestep gambling regulations. Given the NFL’s ad ban, prediction markets will therefore have to get creative with their Super Bowl marketing strategy. They won’t be able to partner with NFL players or teams like they have in other leagues, because the NFL kiboshed those deals, too. But that doesn’t rule out deals with creators and celebrities, news publisher partnerships or live activations in the greater Los Angeles area, where this season’s Big Game will take place. But in order for agentic shopping to really take off, retailers need to be on board – and, so far, the response has been mixed. Amazon, for instance, has been blocking Muse since shortly after it launched, in part to keep shoppers within its own recommendation and discovery channels. https://anthropic.com/news/public-benefi.body: Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new wholly owned entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline. As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company. The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations. One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them. We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as an LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad. Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit. This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones. In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-lea.body: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt. Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data. To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching. For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance. For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock. Where inference cost comes from Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens. Prompt cache duration Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration. For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching, which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching. This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it: { "cachePoint": { "type": "default", "ttl": "1h" } } For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control. A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times. These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. Tokenomics at scale: Track and cap Amazon Bedrock spend per IAM principal with CUR 2.0 and AWS Budgets Generative AI spend is hard to attribute. Before an organization expands AI access, CFOs and CTOs usually want three answers: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there. In our previous post, Tokenomics at Scale: How Jamf Built Real-Time Spend Enforcement for Amazon Bedrock, we explained a custom enforcement loop built on AWS IAM Identity Center, Amazon Athena over Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs, and AWS Lambda. This approach gives near-real-time control, but it requires code you then own and operate. This post shows how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. The approach relies on three things: IAM principal attribution, which Amazon Bedrock records automatically; AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 or AWS Cost Explorer for reporting; and AWS Budgets with budget actions for enforcement. By the end, you will have per-identity cost reporting and an automatic guardrail that restricts Amazon Bedrock access when a threshold is crossed. Solution overview The solution has three parts: attribute, report, and enforce. Attribute. Amazon Bedrock captures the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal identity, the IAM user or role, for every inference request. This happens automatically, with no change to your Amazon Bedrock model inference calls. If several people share one role, you add per-user detail with session tags passed at role assumption time. If each person or application has its own role, principal tags on the role are enough. Report. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags, then read the data either in Cost Explorer for a console-only view, or in a CUR 2.0 data export for detailed line-item analysis and SQL queries. Enforce. Create an AWS Budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock and filtered to one identity or tag value, then attach a budget action that applies a Deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed. Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself. In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land: A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces. A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint. A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update. We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository. How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circuit computes correctly most of the time and wrong only under stress: high temperature, voltage droop, or specific operand patterns. Because the arithmetic logic path has no ECC or parity (unlike memory), the wrong result, say 4.0001 instead of 4.0000, is never flagged, and it flows through activations and gradients into every replica’s weights. https://databricks.com/blog/how-h6ai-bui.body: Traditional accounts payable and invoice processing tools often force companies into a trade-off: moving quickly using AI automation and risk losing control, or maintaining tedious manual oversight. H6.ai was founded to solve this problem. H6.ai automates accounts payable on top of a company's existing ERP. It reads each invoice, matches it to a purchase order, assigns its lines to the right accounts and checks it against the company's own policies. Our approach combines AI-assisted understanding with approved, deterministic and auditable policy execution. Our challenge was finding a backend solution that could support frequent regression testing at scale. In this industry, no two customers look alike. Each has its own ERP, suppliers, purchase orders, chart of accounts and policies. Invoices range from a one-line service bill to documents with hundreds of lines. And the data keeps moving. At 10 AM an invoice matches an open purchase order with enough quantity left. By the afternoon that order may be partly consumed, amended or closed. Process the same invoice again and the answer changes, even though our code has not. That makes regression testing hard. When a result changes, we need to know whether our change caused it or the customer's data did. Our engineering team needed a scalable solution that could isolate our customers' data and allow us to investigate errors. After learning about the lakebase architecture which separates storage from compute, scales idle compute to zero, and enables branching, we selected it as the core system of record for our platform. Today, every H6.ai customer has a dedicated Lakebase Postgres database. It holds their whole financial context: purchase orders and suppliers synced from the ERP, the chart of accounts and dimensions, past transactions, and their H6 policies. A database per customer keeps each customer's data isolated. It also allows us to freeze snapshots. A Lakebase branch is a copy-on-write copy of a database at a point in time. Creating one copies no data: the branch shares storage with its parent and only stores what changes on it. When we find an invoice H6 handled incorrectly, we branch that customer's database and keep the branch as a snapshot. A purchase order that was open stays open in the snapshot, with the same remaining quantities and prices, even after the ERP closes it. The same holds for suppliers, accounts, dimensions, history and policy settings. We no longer try to recreate the conditions behind an issue. We keep them. Every box in the shaded band is a branch of the same customer database. The harness branches the live database once to take a snapshot and never writes to it. Everything a test writes stays on its own run branch and is deleted with it. Each test case in our harness pairs one invoice with one snapshot and the outcome we expect: which purchase order it should match, which accounts its lines belong to, and whether it should be held for review. https://developers.googleblog.com/catch-.body: I help lead Google's agent skills program, currently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills. To keep that many skill files consistent, I wrote skill-lint, a standalone Go CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated line edits before they ship. Even with skill-lint's own unit and fuzz test suite, a small slice or line-number mistake inside its Markdown parsers or edit applier can sit dormant until an unusual file or edit range triggers a runtime panic in the linter. In Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out. To hunt for crashes, I compiled key functions from my code to see which panic traps survived optimization, and Gemini 4 Argon translated the path to each trap into rules for the Z3 constraint solver. An LLM-written solver model isn't a sound proof system, but it gives the agent an independent way to reason about control flow and synthesize concrete Go reproducers, and every crash it finds is real because go test runs the offending bytes directly. That workflow caught all three bugs I planted in test parsers and turned up three latent bugs in skill-lint. In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow. A recent post from Anthropic showed how formal verification catches latent bugs in C and C++ by having frontier AI models write machine-checked Rocq proofs across OSS-Fuzz libraries. Instead of sampling random inputs like a fuzzer, a formal tool works backward from each failure condition to solve for the exact input that triggers it. Full theorem proving is still too heavy for most day-to-day Go projects, so I wanted to see how much of that bug-hunting power an agent can get from an LLM and a constraint solver in about a minute per function. In C and C++, reading or writing past the end of a buffer corrupts memory. Go catches out-of-bounds access at runtime instead, compiling every slice or index operation it can't prove safe into an explicit branch to runtime.panicBounds that panics, crashing the process unless recovered. Before generating machine code, Go's SSA prove pass already eliminates most of those checks by tracking slice lengths and loop variables. That optimization pass leaves behind only the runtime.panicBounds traps the compiler couldn't rule out on its own, giving the solver a short list of candidate crash sites to target. Security tools tend to look good on tests their own team wrote, so we ran five non-Google-written, public agent-security benchmarks through Agent Anomaly Detection without changing anything. The first was around 2014; he had already seen that the future of Nvidia was in AI, and was full throttle in getting Nvidia as deeply embedded in AI as possible. In recent years I grew frustrated with his increasing tendency to hype things, and a lot of the circular financing worried me, but I never ceased to marvel at the tremendous pivot he had made from powering video games to powering the AI revolution. But nonetheless, he had to go. He enabled and even lobbied for Chinese AI, subverted US policy, and carelessly left himself vulnerable to both blackmail and espionage. His blindness to conflict of interest (or the appearance thereof) cost many people dearly. He acted to the peril of his company, his industry, and his country. He also left Nvidia open to endless litigation and investigation, which is perhaps part of why they encouraged him to go, despite his enormous talents. Replacing him will be a huge blow, but keeping him on was no longer tenable, either. § Yesterday, anticipating today’s outcome I wrote, “If Jensen is indeed on his way out—and Nvidia may really not have much choice to let him go given the potential liability and reputational damage, to say nothing of the scrutiny from investigations if they don’t act—all hell may break loose.” The stock was down 8% in premarket then, now it is down 13, as I write this at the opening bell. I added that “The bigger issue for the AI world at large is that Jensen is the ringmaster of all the insane circular financing. And all that might collapse.” That’s a very real possibility now. I also added “One immediate big question, if he does in fact go, would be whether an Nvidia with an acting CEO (perhaps the CFO?) still goes through with the billions they promised Anthropic in the IPO.” That is now front and center. Things will clearly never be the same, neither for Nvidia, nor the AI industry as a whole. Congressional investigations will continue. The market may crash. China is perhaps the biggest immediate winner here. China hawks will come out force. The politics will be intense. Lutnick and Trump may be caught in the crossfire. The main thing to expect is chaos.

Eine weitreichende Störung bei Microsoft 365 beeinträchtigt momentan weltweit zahlreiche Cloud-Dienste. Neben Exchange Online sind auch Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Defender XDR wie auch for Office 365, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft To Do, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Purview und Power BI potenziell betroffen. Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige Nutzer können womöglich auf mehrere Microsoft-365-Dienste nicht zugreifen. Seit dem frühen Abend hiesiger Zeit fielen „unerwartet viele Server“ aus, was beim Rest zu Überlastung geführt haben dürfte; erste Störungsberichte kamen aus den USA. Update 12.11.2026, 22:57 Uhr Die Liste der betroffenen Cloud-Dienste Microsoft wird länger und länger, wir haben den ersten Absatz angepasst. Unterdessen entspannt sich die Lage. Beispielsweise kann Microsoft Exchange wieder eingehende E-Mails verarbeiten, je nach Örtlichkeit kann es dabei noch zu Verzögerungen kommen. Microsoft teilt mit, die betroffenen Server der Reihe nach zu Prüfung und neu zu starten. Dabei sucht der Datenkonzern nach einer Möglichkeit, diesen Prozess zu beschleunigen. Zudem hat das Unternehmen eine „kleine Anzahl“ jüngst durchgeführter Konfigurationsänderungen gefunden; derzeit untersucht es, ob deren Rückgängigmachung die Wiederaufnahme des Normalbetriebes beschleunigen kann. Update 12.11.2026, 23:38 Uhr Microsoft sucht nach neuen Ansätzen, da „unsere Maßnahmen bislang nicht die erwartete Entspannung gebracht haben.“ Wie sich herausstellt, wird ein Kernprozss der Server überlastet, was zu deren Absturz und unzulänglichen Cloud-Kapazitäten führt. Daher isoliert Microsoft nun einen Teil seiner Infrastruktur, startet die betroffenen Teile neu und steigert nur behutsam den ihnen zugeleiteten Datenverkehr, um die Auswirkungen beobachten zu können. Parallel analysiert der Datenkonzern die Datenverkehrsmuster in seiner gesamten Cloud um herauszufinden, ob sich einzelne Cloudregionen eigenständig erfangen, wenn sie nur Datenverkehr aus der eigenen geographischen Region verarbeiten müssen. „Unerwartet viele Server ausgefallen“ Laut dem aktuellen Status-Update von Microsoft wird die erhöhte Last auf der Infrastruktur nicht durch einen allgemeinen Traffic-Anstieg verursacht. Stattdessen ist eine ungewöhnlich große Anzahl an Servern unerwartet ausgefallen. Dadurch wird die Last auf die verbleibende Infrastruktur verlagert, was zu Verbindungsfehlern bei den Nutzern führt. Wie aus früheren Updates hervorgeht, scheitern die betroffenen Server an automatisierten Health-Checks. Die Untersuchungen deuten laut Microsoft darauf hin, dass diese fehlerhaften Health-Checks von einer spezifischen Komponente stammen könnten, die für die Verarbeitung der Serverintegrität verantwortlich ist.
